prompt: What does reading the document `customers/c-17` return?
hint: A subcollection is not stored inside its parent.

choices.text: Only the customer's own fields
choices.why: Right. The `orders` subcollection is read separately.

choices.text: The customer's fields and every order under it
choices.why: Orders in a subcollection are not part of the parent document.

choices.text: A list of the subcollection names
choices.why: Listing collections under a document is a separate call.

choices.text: Nothing until the collection is created
choices.why: Collections are created by writing a document into them.

prompt: Why does Quitanda not keep a customer's orders in an array field of the customer's document?
hint: A document has a size limit.

choices.text: Arrays cannot be indexed
choices.why: Arrays get an `array-contains` index; the problem is growth.

choices.text: Arrays are read one element per billed read
choices.why: A document read is one read, whatever its size.

choices.text: It grows towards the 1 MiB limit
choices.why: Right. A subcollection has no size limit, which is what it is for.

choices.text: Batches cannot write arrays
choices.why: `seed.py` writes `products`, an array, in a batch.

prompt: How many bytes may one field's value hold in Firestore, as the emulator's refusal said?
An order stores the path of a product document, and the product is deleted. What does Firestore do?

choices.text: Refuses the delete while orders refer to it
choices.why: That is a foreign key; Firestore has none.

choices.text: Deletes the orders too
choices.why: That is Spanner's `ON DELETE CASCADE`; Firestore has no cascade.

choices.text: Moves the orders to a deleted-products collection
choices.why: Firestore moves nothing on its own.

choices.text: Nothing; the path now leads nowhere
choices.why: Right. A reference is a value, and integrity is the program's job.

prompt: Which indexes does Firestore build automatically for a field in a collection?
hint: Two directions, and one more for arrays.

choices.text: None; every index is declared
choices.why: Single-field indexes are automatic.

choices.text: Both directions, plus `array-contains`
choices.why: Right. These are the single-field indexes.

choices.text: Only the document id
choices.why: Every field is indexed unless exempted.

choices.text: One composite index per pair of fields
choices.why: Composite indexes are declared, never built by themselves.

prompt: Every new click document has a `clicked_at` timestamp, and the app writes thousands a second to one collection. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: A value that grows with every write.

choices.text: Add a composite index on `clicked_at`
choices.why: More index entries at the end of the same range make it worse.

choices.text: A stale read before each write
choices.why: Reads do not change where index entries land.

choices.text: An exemption for `clicked_at`
choices.why: Right. A sequential indexed value caps the collection near 500 writes a second.

choices.text: Write the clicks in a transaction
choices.why: A transaction adds work; the hotspot is the index.

prompt: Why does `query.py` end every query with `limit(5)`?

choices.text: Each returned document is billed
choices.why: Right. The limit names the price. Without it a query pays for everything that matches.

choices.text: The emulator returns at most five documents
choices.why: The emulator returns everything that matches.

choices.text: Collection group queries need a limit
choices.why: They do not; the limit is a choice.

choices.text: Indexes hold only five entries per value
choices.why: An index holds an entry per document.

prompt: `pending-biggest` answered on the laptop. What happens on its first call against Firestore with no composite index?
hint: The emulator's default mode checks no index.

choices.text: It answers the same rows, more slowly
choices.why: Firestore has no slow path; it refuses.

choices.text: It scans the collection group and bills every document
choices.why: Firestore never scans.

choices.text: Firestore builds the index on the fly
choices.why: Composite indexes are declared, and building one takes time.

choices.text: It fails, and the error links to the index to create
choices.why: Right. That is the refusal the Native emulator never gives.

prompt: The composite index for `pending-biggest` is created with the default `--query-scope=collection`. Which query does it serve?
hint: Which collections does the query read?

choices.text: `pending-biggest`, as written in `query.py`
choices.why: That reads the collection group, and needs the collection-group scope.

choices.text: The same query on one customer's `orders`
choices.why: Right. Collection scope serves a query on one collection.

choices.text: Every query on `status`
choices.why: Single-field queries already have their indexes.

choices.text: Queries in Datastore mode only
choices.why: Scope is about collections, not modes.

prompt: How can the laptop be made to refuse a query that lacks a composite index?
hint: One mode has a flag for it.

choices.text: Datastore mode, with `--require-indexes`
choices.why: Right. With `--index-file` beside it; the help says both work only in Datastore mode.

choices.text: Start the Native emulator with `--rules`
choices.why: Rules are about access, not indexes.

choices.text: Set `FIRESTORE_EMULATOR_HOST` to port 8081
choices.why: That only changes where the client connects.

choices.text: Use Query Explain before each query
choices.why: The emulator returns no explain metrics.

prompt: Firestore's feature that reports the index used and the documents read by a query, which the emulator does not provide, is Query ___.
hint: It is spelt like the SQL keyword for a plan.

prompt: In `stock.py`, why was the losing customer refused rather than allowed to buy six?

choices.text: Firestore refuses a second write
choices.why: The winner's write was the second write to a document read twice.

choices.text: The thread started later
choices.why: Both started together; the commit order decided.

choices.text: Batches cannot decrement a field
choices.why: This is a transaction, and it reads before it writes.

choices.text: Its transaction ran again from the top and read four
choices.why: Right. Retried from the top, it saw the stock as it now was.

prompt: A page of 10 orders is fetched with `offset(90).limit(10)`. By the pricing page's rule, how many document reads are billed?
Every order also increments one `stats/today` document, and at the evening peak orders arrive several per second. What is the problem, and the fix?
hint: A single document has a sustained write rate.

choices.text: No problem; transactions serialise the increments
choices.why: They do, which is the problem: one document takes about one write a second.

choices.text: The document grows past 1 MiB; split it by hour
choices.why: A counter does not grow; the rate is the issue.

choices.text: One document: about one write a second
choices.why: Right. Spread the counter over several documents, a distributed counter added up on read.

choices.text: Index exemptions on the counter field
choices.why: Indexes are not the limit here; the document is.

prompt: At 0.045 USD per 100,000 reads beyond 50,000 free a day, what do 250,000 reads a day cost over 30 days, in USD?
Which Quitanda database fits Datastore mode rather than Native?

choices.text: The app's order history, read from phones
choices.why: Phones need the Firebase SDKs, which are Native mode's.

choices.text: A service only servers read
choices.why: Right. Servers lose nothing without listeners and mobile SDKs.

choices.text: The delivery status screen, which listens for changes
choices.why: Real-time listeners are Native mode's.

choices.text: Any database with more than 1 GiB
choices.why: Size does not choose the mode.

prompt: Quitanda moves the app's data from the `(default)` database to a named database `shop`, with the same traffic. What happens to the monthly bill of 4.86?
hint: Read what the free quota applies to.

choices.text: Nothing; the free quota is per project
choices.why: The page says named databases do not qualify for it.

choices.text: It falls, because named databases cost less
choices.why: The rates are the same; only the free quota differs.

choices.text: It doubles, because both databases are billed
choices.why: The `(default)` database would be empty and cost nothing.

choices.text: It rises: no free quota for named databases
choices.why: Right. Every read, write and GiB is then billed from the first one.

prompt: Match each Firestore term to its Datastore-mode name or meaning.
hint: Datastore had its own words first.

pairs.right: a declared index over several properties

prompt: Which of these did the Firestore emulator in Native mode do as Firestore would? Choose all that apply.
hint: Data model and transactions, or indexes and metrics?

choices.text: Refuse a field value over 1,048,487 bytes
choices.why: Yes; the limit is Firestore's.

choices.text: Retry a transaction whose read went stale
choices.why: Yes; the stock never went below zero.

choices.text: Page with a cursor from the last document
choices.why: Yes; `pages.py` read six pages.

choices.text: Refuse a query that needs a missing composite index
choices.why: Only Datastore mode with `--require-indexes` refused.

choices.text: Return Query Explain metrics
choices.why: It returned none.

prompt: Put the steps of shipping `pending-biggest` to production in order.
hint: The index has to exist before the query meets it.
items: Write the query and run it against the emulator
Declare the composite index with collection-group scope
Wait for the index to finish building
Deploy the code that runs the query
